extracted.intended_audience: government regulators, policy-makers, regulatory oversight bodies, and institutional designers in OECD member and partner countries
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, implementing and evaluating regulatory systems, including oversight, stakeholder engagement, regulatory impact assessment (RIA) and ex post evaluation. Aimed at institutions that create, review or monitor regulation (executive, oversight bodies, legislatures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design clear, coherent, and efficient regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should be designed to be clear, coherent and efficient so they can support economic growth, social welfare and environmental protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat regulation as a tool to achieve policy objectives; avoid unnecessary complexity or overlap. Emphasise clarity of rules and minimising undue burdens on regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectively implement regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory regimes must be effectively implemented by competent authorities so that intended policy outcomes are realised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation requires managerial capacity, training, and institutional arrangements that enable consistent application; oversight bodies often play a role in supporting implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continually evaluate regulations for appropriateness, relevance and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should be subject to ongoing ex post evaluation to assess whether they remain appropriate, relevant and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make evaluation a continuous part of the regulatory lifecycle rather than a one-off exercise; use findings to adapt or remove regulations where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a holistic regulatory ecosystem: connect institutions, tools and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory institutions, tools and processes should be ‘connected’ so instruments (oversight, stakeholder engagement, RIA, ex post evaluation) form a coherent ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View instruments as means to an end and employ them as part of an integrated system that supports evidence-based policy-making rather than as separate exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt instruments to the administrative and institutional context
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single blueprint for regulatory practice — instruments must be tailored to each country’s administrative, institutional context and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and use instruments (oversight, RIA, consultations, evaluation) adapted to local constraints (e.g., strong centre vs consensus-based administration), rather than transplanting models unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for institutional setup and administrative culture in oversight design
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory oversight arrangements should reflect the specific institutional constellation (e.g., presidential vs parliamentary systems) and administrative culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The range of tools and methods used by oversight bodies will vary with institutional set-up; choices should recognise delegation/accountability chains and incentives across actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight bodies should provide guidance, direction and training to regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Oversight often includes managerial tasks: providing regulatory guidance, direction, and training to ministries and agencies that design and implement regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight should not be purely permissive or punitive — it should build capacity in line ministries to apply good regulatory practice tools (RIA, consultations, ex post evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include legislatures in regulatory quality processes and quality checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures play a key role in designing policies and overseeing implementation, and should be included in regulatory quality processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed quality checks and review functions in legislative procedures as well as in the executive to strengthen accountability and results-orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on reactive complaint-driven stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying excessively on reactive, complaint-driven approaches (businesses/citizens flagging implemented problems) reduces incentives for governments to proactively diagnose and learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement complaint-driven mechanisms with upstream engagement and systematic approaches to identify regulatory bottlenecks before problems crystallise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure inclusiveness and effectiveness in stakeholder engagement; use consultation plans and stakeholder mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder engagement exercises must balance inclusiveness and practical effectiveness; tools such as consultation plans and stakeholder mapping help achieve this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map stakeholder experience with services/regulation to identify who to involve and design consultations that are accessible and targeted to the issue and stage of policy development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate stakeholder engagement from procurement of scientific/technical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder engagement is distinct from commissioning scientific or technical expertise; both are important but not substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experts to inform technical questions and broad stakeholder consultations to capture affected parties’ views, lived experience and practical alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement is required at every phase of ex post evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders should be involved in selection of evaluation targets, assessment of effectiveness and burdens, searching for alternatives, and analysis of impacts of alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders often have the best information on impacts and feasible alternatives — build engagement into each stage of ex post review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce stakeholder engagement through review mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Because regulators often lack incentives to engage stakeholders, engagement needs to be enforced or incentivised via review and oversight mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design review rules and oversight checks that require or reward stakeholder consultation; avoid leaving engagement optional or purely discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post evaluations should be conducted only when benefits exceed costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to resource constraints, ex post evaluations are justified only if expected benefits of the evaluation exceed the costs of conducting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise reviews with higher expected net benefits; use triage mechanisms to identify which regulations merit deeper analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose efficient review approaches: review depth, multi-stage reviews, and stakeholder use
rubrics_metrics.description: Given limited resources, authorities should select an appropriate depth of review, use multi-stage (screening then deeper analysis) reviews, and leverage stakeholder input to reduce information costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with lighter-weight reviews to prioritise and then escalate to more quantitative or detailed examinations where justified; Regulatory Reform Sinmungo is cited as an example of multi-stage review in Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply sunset provisions selectively when a review is expected to be beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunset rules should be used in a targeted way — apply a sunset provision only where a review is likely to be valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket sunset rules that create unnecessary review burdens; use sunset to focus attention on regulations with uncertain continuing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost-in Cost-out (CICO) to provide internal incentives to regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: CICO systems (cost-in, cost-out) can give regulators incentives to seek less burdensome alternatives by banking the savings from abolished/relaxed regulations to offset future regulatory costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CICO can complement other review mechanisms by creating internal budgetary incentives for regulatory quality and burden reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory oversight must monitor and manage ex post evaluations; external incentives are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Because regulators have weak incentives to improve regulations, oversight bodies (e.g., Regulatory Reform Committee, Prime Minister’s Office, Ministerial Meeting on Regulatory Reform) should monitor and manage ex post evaluation systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear oversight channels and reporting lines for ex post evaluation outcomes and follow-up actions; oversight bodies can review evaluation quality and enforce stakeholder engagement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise bundled reviews where individual regulations interact
rubrics_metrics.description: Some regulations may appear rational in isolation but not when reviewed together; bundled reviews are necessary to capture interactions among related regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regulatory planning, principles-based reviews or cross-ministry initiatives to examine sets of related regulations rather than only individual instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regulatory planning and review to order existing regulations by importance and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory planning should classify and order existing regulations by their importance and expected benefit to identify candidates for abolition or deeper review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory planning can feed into CICO and sunset decisions by providing a prioritized list of regulations for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design an optimal mix of review mechanisms recognising complementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different review mechanisms (CICO, regulatory planning, stock-flow linkages, principles-based reviews, bottom-up proposals) are complementary; choose an optimal mix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage strengths of each mechanism and coordinate them so information from one (e.g., stakeholder proposals) informs others (e.g., planning, CICO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use light triage reviews to efficiently allocate scarce evaluation resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform simple initial reviews to rank regulations for necessity of further, deeper analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A light-touch screening stage reduces wasted effort and focuses resources where quantitative analysis will meaningfully change decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise stakeholders as primary sources of information on regulatory impacts and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders often better understand the practical effects and feasible alternatives to regulation, making their input essential for high-quality reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively solicit and use stakeholder data during selection, assessment and design of alternatives to improve the accuracy and relevance of ex post evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design oversight and stakeholder engagement to counter regulators' incentives to strengthen regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators may have biases toward strengthening regulation; oversight and stakeholder engagement can act as counterbalancing forces to promote efficiency without eroding effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine external oversight checks with empowered stakeholder inputs to constrain unjustified regulatory strengthening and encourage evidence-based changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transparency of regulatory improvement plans and review outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory planning and the final versions of improvement plans should be open to the public to allow stakeholder preview, scrutiny and agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure increases accountability and the likelihood that stakeholder concerns are captured; the report notes some Korean planning processes were not open and thus limited stakeholder influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply quantitative RIA methods proportionately when they materially improve decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantification and monetisation (cost-benefit analysis, EANDCB, other methods) in RIAs when these analyses are likely to materially improve review results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative analysis is costly; require it where expected gains justify the effort, and otherwise rely on qualitative or lighter-weight methods. Note: the report observes some systems (e.g., Korea) do not formally require quantitative analysis.
